key_insight: Implementing AI in maternal health depends less on the algorithm itself and more on strengthening data quality, workflow design, and local health-system capacity.
clinical_relevance: For high-risk pregnancy screening, ML can only support care when routine measurements, documentation, referral pathways, and follow-up actions are reliable and usable in real practice.
method: Retrospective mixed-methods implementation analysis in Geita, Tanzania (2022–2024)
Triangulated exit interviews, focus groups, key informant interviews, routine system data, and project records
Used abductive analysis with the NASSS framework plus a study-specific ML implementation pathway
evidence_signal: The study combined endline evaluation findings with quantitative and qualitative data from women, healthcare workers, routine UCS records, and documented ML development experience.
watch_item: A key concern is that staffing shortages and extra confirmatory work can create new burdens, so AI may not scale without clear workflow redesign and local ownership.
paper_title: What it takes to implement AI in Africa: health-system lessons from developing an ML-enabled maternal risk stratification algorithm in Tanzania
